screens.title: Advanced Routing & NAT
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this lesson you will build a mental toolbox for advanced routing and NAT that you will use as an RHCA. We begin by grounding static routing: why you still need it in a world of dynamic protocols, and how a single static route can direct a server to an isolated subnet or VPN peer. Then we expand to policy-based routing, which allows you to make routing decisions based on source address, UID, or interface — useful for multi‑homed servers and service segregation. You will also learn practical nftables NAT recipes: source NAT and masquerading for outbound internet access, DNAT for port forwarding, and the niche but important NPTv6 for prefix translation. Lastly, we touch on the role of dynamic protocols at scale and the troubleshooting commands you will use to verify behavior. Expect concrete examples you can copy into your lab, troubleshooting checks to avoid common mistakes, and a hands-on scenario where a gateway serves internal hosts while forwarding selected services. By the end you should be able to explain why a static route or a PBR rule was chosen, write the right nftables NAT rule, and verify packet flow. How would you choose between static routes, policy rules, or a routing daemon in your next design?

screens.title: Static Routing: Deterministic paths
screens.narratorSegment: Static routing is a manually configured instruction that tells the kernel to use a specific next hop for a destination. It is not learned from neighbors; it is authoritative and predictable. You use static routes for isolated subnets, tunnel endpoints, and simple failover where a deterministic path is required. For example, if a server must reach 10.0.0.0/24 through 192.168.1.254 on interface eth0, you add a static route that pins that traffic to that gateway. A frequent mistake is adding the route to the wrong interface or not persisting it, which causes problems after a reboot. Persisting a static route on RHEL often uses NetworkManager configuration so the route survives reconnects. Another misconception is that static routes are obsolete because dynamic routing exists; in practice, static routes are simpler and safer for single host policies and for ensuring control over particular flows. In this screen you'll see the command example and a persistence recipe; practice will help you move from adding transient routes to designing a stable routing table that supports VPNs and isolated services. Ask yourself: when would a static route be better than learning the path from a routing daemon?

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.6 › Static Routing
Definition

Static route explained

A static route is a fixed kernel entry that sends traffic for a given prefix to a chosen next hop. It does not change unless you edit it, making troubleshooting straightforward when predictability is required.

Common use: VPN endpoints, isolated subnets, or backup links.
Misconception: Static means "set and forget"—you must still validate reachability when interfaces or gateways change.
Key Takeaway

Use static routes for predictable paths and persist them using NetworkManager or configuration files. Always verify with ip route get.

Code example
# Add a static route using ip command (temporary)
sudo ip route add 10.0.0.0/24 via 192.168.1.254 dev eth0

# Make it persistent using nmcli
sudo nmcli connection modify eth0 +ipv4.routes "10.0.0.0/24 192.168.1.254"
sudo nmcli connection up eth0
Example scenario
A server with a VPN peer that only reaches a management subnet via a separate gateway. A static route ensures the management subnet traffic never goes to the default gateway and avoids route flapping.
Check your work
  • Use ip route get to confirm the path.
  • Restart the connection and confirm persistent routes come back.
  • Watch for incorrect interface names or typos in gateway addresses.

screens.title: Policy-Based Routing (PBR)
screens.narratorSegment: Policy-based routing lets you make routing decisions using criteria other than the destination address. The two core components are ip rules and routing tables. An ip rule matches a condition — for example, a source address or a UID — and points to a named routing table. That table contains routes used only when the rule matches. A typical flow is: create a table entry in /etc/iproute2/rt_tables, add routes to that table, then create an ip rule to direct matching traffic to it. For example, traffic from 192.168.1.100 can be forced out a separate gateway, preserving the default route for other hosts. PBR is powerful for multi‑homed hosts, VPN exit selection, and isolating application traffic. A frequent pitfall is incorrect rule priority ordering or not verifying the rule with ip rule show; another is forgetting that policy rules are consulted before regular routing, so an overly broad rule can capture traffic unintentionally. Practice by adding a table, a route in that table, and an ip rule, then simulate a lookup with ip route get specifying the source to confirm behavior. Consider: which applications benefit most from PBR in your environment?

keyIdea.title: PBR essentials
keyIdea.text: Create a routing table, add routes to it, and add ip rules to match traffic by source, UID, or interface. Use ip rule show to inspect active policies.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.6 › Policy-Based Routing
Process

PBR setup steps

1. Add a table name
Append an entry to the routing tables file so the table can be referenced by name or number.
2. Add routes to that table
Populate the custom table with specific routes and a default gateway for that traffic class.
3. Create ip rules
Add ip rules that match source addresses, UID ranges, or interfaces to direct traffic to your custom table.
4. Verify and simulate
Inspect active rules with ip rule show and use ip route get from a source to confirm the lookup result.
Example
# Example overview (see chapter for exact commands)
# 1. Add table name
sudo echo "100 custom_route" | sudo tee -a /etc/iproute2/rt_tables

# 2. Add route to the table
sudo ip route add default via 172.16.1.1 dev eth1 table custom_route

# 3. Create a rule for source
sudo ip rule add from 192.168.1.100 table custom_route
Analogy
Think of the kernel as a librarian: ip rules are signs that tell the librarian which shelf (routing table) to consult for specific books (packets) based on who brings them in.
Common Mistake

Adding rules without verifying priority can cause unintended capture of traffic. Always inspect ip rule show order.

screens.title: nftables SNAT and Masquerade
screens.narratorSegment: Source NAT changes the source address of outbound packets so replies return to the gateway and reach the original sender. In practice you either set a specific public address with SNAT or use masquerading when the outbound address is dynamic. Using nftables you place SNAT or masquerade rules in the postrouting chain of the nat table. For example, to translate 192.168.0.0/24 to a fixed public IP you write an snat rule; to automatically use whatever IP the interface holds you use masquerade. A common error is applying the rule to the wrong interface name or forgetting to enable IP forwarding in the kernel. For hands-on verification, load the ruleset and then use tcpdump on the external interface to confirm packets carry the translated source and check connection tracking entries. Below is the nftables rule example from the chapter for both specific SNAT and masquerade. Practice by toggling between a fixed snat address and masquerade to see how replies are handled when the external IP changes. nftables SNAT and Masquerade means snat sets a specific public ip; masquerade uses the interface ip dynamically. use masquerade for pppoe or dhcp-assigned public addresses.. In practical terms, configure source nat for outbound connectivity and understand masquerading. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: SNAT vs Masquerade
keyIdea.text: SNAT sets a specific public IP; masquerade uses the interface IP dynamically. Use masquerade for PPPoE or DHCP-assigned public addresses.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.6 › SNAT & Masquerade
Concept

Source NAT behavior

SNAT rewrites packet source addresses so return traffic arrives at the translator. Masquerade is a form of SNAT that uses the outbound interface address dynamically. Both are applied after routing, in postrouting chains.

  • Enable net.ipv4.ip_forward for routed NAT traffic to pass.
  • Place SNAT/masquerade in the nat table postrouting chain.
  • Verify translations with nft list ruleset and tcpdump on the external interface.
nftables example
table ip nat {
    chain postrouting {
        type nat hook postrouting priority 100; policy accept;
        oifname "eth0" ip saddr 192.168.0.0/24 snat to 203.0.113.10 # Specific public IP
        # OR for dynamic IP:
        # oifname "eth0" ip saddr 192.168.0.0/24 masquerade
    }
}
Practice: switch between a fixed snat address and masquerade to observe the differences when the outward IP changes.

screens.title: DNAT and Port Forwarding with nftables
screens.narratorSegment: Destination NAT changes the destination address of inbound packets so external clients can reach internal services. Use DNAT when you want to publish a web server behind a gateway. DNAT rules belong in the prerouting chain of the nat table because the destination must be rewritten before the kernel performs routing decisions. A correct DNAT includes matching the incoming interface, the gateway's public IP or any destination address, and the TCP port to forward. A typical error is forgetting to allow forwarded packets through the filter forward chain or neglecting to permit established and related states. After creating the rule, verify that the prerouting translation happens by listing the nftables ruleset and capturing packets on both external and internal interfaces to see original and translated destinations. The chapter includes a concrete example mapping external port 80 to an internal host on port 80; practice this with a non-production server and ensure firewall forward rules permit the flow. Think: what other services may require DNAT and what security controls should accompany them? DNAT and Port Forwarding with nftables means place dnat in prerouting, allow forwarding in filter chains, verify with nft list ruleset and tcpdump, and test service reachability from an external client.. In practical terms, expose internal services safely using prerouting dnat. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.6 › DNAT / Port Forwarding
Definition

DNAT behavior and risks

DNAT rewrites destination addresses so external requests arrive at internal servers. Because this exposes internal services, pair DNAT with strict filter rules and service-level security controls. DNAT must be applied before routing decisions.

  • Use prerouting chain in nat table for DNAT.
  • Open the forward chain for translated flows and allow established states.
  • Confirm correct matching of external IP and port to avoid accidental wide-open forwarding.
nftables DNAT example
table ip nat {
    chain prerouting {
        type nat hook prerouting priority -100; policy accept;
        iifname "eth0" tcp dport 80 dnat to 192.168.0.10:80
    }
}
Tip: After adding DNAT, ensure your forward chain allows new established traffic between external and internal interfaces.

screens.title: NPTv6: IPv6 Prefix Translation
screens.narratorSegment: Network Prefix Translation for IPv6, known as NPTv6, maps one IPv6 prefix to another in a deterministic, reversible way. Unlike IPv4 NAT that rewrites host addresses arbitrarily, NPTv6 translates prefixes on a one-to-one basis, preserving the address scheme inside while allowing external renumbering or multi‑homing. This is useful when changing providers or when internal numbering must remain stable across provider changes. Because IPv6 has abundant addresses, NPTv6 is less common but still valuable in multi‑homed designs where you cannot use provider-independent addressing. nftables supports NPTv6 rules; implement them carefully since they affect routing and potential firewall policies. A misconception is expecting NPTv6 to behave like IPv4 NAT for port sharing — it is prefix based and intended for symmetry rather than hiding hosts. Test in a lab by translating an internal prefix to an external prefix, then validate with ping and tcpdump to confirm that address translations follow the expected mapping and that connection tracking reflects consistent state. NPTv6: IPv6 Prefix Translation means nptv6 maps one ipv6 prefix to another for renumbering or multi-homing; it is prefix-preserving and reversible, not a port-level nat.. In practical terms, when and how to translate ipv6 prefixes without traditional nat drawbacks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.6 › NPTv6
What NPTv6 does
It replaces an internal IPv6 prefix with an external one so internal addresses remain stable while outward addressing changes. NPTv6 is useful for renumbering and certain multi-homing scenarios.
When to use it
Use NPTv6 when you cannot renumber internal hosts but need to change provider prefixes or present a consistent external addressing plan for multi-homing.
Misconception
NPTv6 is not a port-forwarding tool. It preserves host identifiers inside the prefix mapping and is intended for prefix-level translation.
Verification
Validate with ping and tcpdump. Confirm that the translated packets use the mapped prefix and that connection tracking remains coherent.

screens.title: OSPF vs BGP (Conceptual)
screens.narratorSegment: As an RHCA you must know when to recommend dynamic routing daemons like OSPF or BGP versus host-level static or policy routing. OSPF is an interior gateway protocol used inside an autonomous system. It builds a link-state database so routers learn the network topology and compute shortest paths. BGP, in contrast, is an exterior gateway protocol used between autonomous systems; it shares path and policy information and selects routes based on path attributes and policy rather than shortest path metrics. A common design pattern is to let routers run OSPF inside a datacenter and use BGP between data centers or to the internet. However, for a single host or small gateway, running a routing daemon may add complexity; static routes or PBR are often simpler and more controllable. Misconception: BGP is not only for the internet; it is also used for large private networks requiring policy-based inter-domain routing. Think about scale, change rate, and policy needs when choosing between static, PBR, OSPF, or BGP. OSPF vs BGP (Conceptual) means use ospf inside stable autonomous systems, bgp for policy-rich external or multi-domain routing; prefer static/pbr for host-level or simple gateway control.. In practical terms, when to recommend an igp or an egp in your architecture. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.6 › OSPF vs BGP
OSPF (IGP)
Link-state protocol used within an autonomous system to compute shortest path routes from a shared topology. Good for converged, internal networks where topology is shared among peers.
BGP (EGP)
Path-vector protocol used between autonomous systems. Makes routing decisions based on path attributes and policy, suitable for inter-domain and internet routing.
When to recommend what
If you need dynamic, policy-rich inter-AS routing use BGP; for internal shortest-path convergence use OSPF. For simple host-level control or a gateway with limited peers, prefer static routes or PBR to avoid extra daemon complexity.

screens.title: Troubleshooting Routing Decisions
screens.narratorSegment: Troubleshooting advanced routing often requires stepping through the kernel's lookup process and verifying what actually hits the wire. Start with ip route get to ask the kernel which route it will use for a specific destination and source. This tells you the selected next hop and interface. Next, inspect ip rule show to see policy-based routing entries that might override the usual destination lookup. For NAT issues, run nft list ruleset to confirm your nat table has the expected prerouting and postrouting entries. Packet capture is the ultimate verification: run tcpdump on both internal and external interfaces to observe original and translated addresses. Watch connection tracking state as well; many NAT problems stem from ct state mismatches or stale entries. A common misconception is that the kernel will always pick the default route; in reality ip rules and table lookups can redirect traffic before the default is consulted. When a packet fails, simulate with ip route get from the source and run tcpdump to confirm whether the packet is leaving the expected interface. Keep a checklist: ip rule show, ip route show table, ip route get, nft list ruleset, tcpdump on both interfaces.

screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the provided hands-on gateway scenario. The gateway has two interfaces: eth0 public with 203.0.113.10/24 and eth1 private with 192.168.100.1/24. The internal webserver is 192.168.100.100. The goals are to enable IP forwarding, configure nftables to masquerade internal outbound traffic, DNAT external port 80 to the internal server, and implement PBR so traffic originating from the webserver uses an alternative internal gateway if present. Start by enabling kernel forwarding, then apply nftables rules that define a nat table with prerouting for DNAT and postrouting for masquerade. Common mistakes include missing forward chain accept rules, wrong interface names, and forgetting to persist nftables. Module 11 › Chapter 11.6 › Gateway Scenario
Scenario summary
Gateway: eth0 public 203.0.113.10, eth1 private 192.168.100.1. Internal webserver: 192.168.100.100. Objectives: enable IP forwarding, DNAT port 80 to webserver, masquerade outbound, and PBR for webserver-originated traffic.
Starter commands
# 1. Enable IP forwarding
sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1
sudo echo "net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1" | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/99-ip-forward.conf

# 2. nftables excerpt: DNAT and masquerade
# see chapter for full file content
Verification steps
  • sudo nft list ruleset — check nat rules in prerouting and postrouting.
  • sudo ip rule show — confirm webserver_pbr entry exists.
  • sudo ip route show table webserver_pbr — verify default via 192.168.100.254.
  • tcpdump on eth0 and eth1 to confirm DNAT and masquerade behavior.
Configuration excerpt
table inet filter {
    chain forward { type filter hook forward priority 0; policy drop;
        iifname "eth1" oifname "eth0" accept
        iifname "eth0" oifname "eth1" ct state new tcp dport 80 accept
    }
}

table ip nat {
    chain prerouting { type nat hook prerouting priority -100; policy accept;
        iifname "eth0" tcp dport 80 dnat to 192.168.100.100:80
    }
    chain postrouting { type nat hook postrouting priority 100; policy accept;
        oifname "eth0" ip saddr 192.168.100.0/24 masquerade
    }
}

screens.title: Implement PBR by UID (assessment idea)
screens.narratorSegment: This guided exercise helps you route traffic for a single application user out a chosen interface by using UID-based policy rules. The technique is valuable when applications must use a designated uplink regardless of the system default. The steps: determine the UID of the user, create a routing table entry pointing to the intended gateway on the desired interface, and add an ip rule uidrange that maps that UID to your custom table. After adding the rule, verify with ip rule show and simulate a lookup with ip route get specifying the UID parameter to confirm which table will be used. A common pitfall is assuming UID rules affect already-established sockets; they only affect new connection attempts. Also remember to persist the routing table entry and rules in your system configuration or a dispatcher script because ip rule and ip route changes do not persist by default. This exercise is the basis of the assessment question where all traffic from a user should leave via eth1 even when the system default points elsewhere. Implement PBR by UID (assessment idea) means use ip rule with uidrange to bind a user's new connections to a custom routing table. verify using ip rule show and ip route get with uid.. In practical terms, route traffic for a given uid out a specific interface using ip rule uidrange. content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.6 › PBR by UID
Exercise goal
Ensure all new connections created by a specific user account exit via eth1, regardless of the system default route.
Steps
  1. Find the UID of the application user.
  2. Add a routing table entry with a default via the intended gateway for eth1.
  3. Add an ip rule uidrange mapping the UID to the custom table.
  4. Verify with ip rule show and ip route get with uid simulation.
Remember: UID rules affect new connections. Existing sockets will not be moved retroactively, so test by restarting the application process.
Starter commands
# Get UID
APPUSER_UID=$(id -u appuser)

# Create table entry
echo "100 appuser_traffic" | sudo tee -a /etc/iproute2/rt_tables
sudo ip route add default via 192.168.B.1 dev eth1 table appuser_traffic

# Add UID-based rule
sudo ip rule add uidrange $APPUSER_UID-$APPUSER_UID table appuser_traffic

# Verify
sudo ip rule show
sudo ip route show table appuser_traffic

screens.title: Safe Deployment Patterns and Pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: When you change routing or NAT on a production gateway, you must follow safe deployment patterns. First, always test in an isolated lab that mirrors interface names and gateway addresses. Use non-production IPs and verify rules with nft list ruleset and tcpdump. Second, persist configuration: ip route and ip rule changes are ephemeral, so write persistent entries via NetworkManager, system startup scripts, or the proper distro configuration so the system recovers after reboots or link flaps. Third, secure DNAT exposures: only forward needed ports and restrict source addresses where possible. Fourth, monitor connection tracking and stale states; NAT relies on a consistent connection tracking table and misconfigured firewall rules can cause half-open or broken connections. Common pitfalls include forgetting to enable ip forwarding, mis-typed interface names, and placing NAT rules in the wrong chain. Finally, include rollback steps and a maintenance window when you apply gateway changes. A simple test plan and verification checklist will save hours of troubleshooting and prevent accidental outages. fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this lesson you will build a mental toolbox for advanced routing and NAT that you will use as an RHCA. We begin by grounding static routing: why you still need it in a world of dynamic protocols, and how a single static route can direct a server to an isolated subnet or VPN peer. Then we expand to policy-based routing, which allows you to make routing decisions based on source address, UID, or interface — useful for multi‑homed servers and service segregation. You will also learn practical nftables NAT recipes: source NAT and masquerading for outbound internet access, DNAT for port forwarding, and the niche but important NPTv6 for prefix translation. Lastly, we touch on the role of dynamic protocols at scale and the troubleshooting commands you will use to verify behavior. Expect concrete examples you can copy into your lab, troubleshooting checks to avoid common mistakes, and a hands-on scenario where a gateway serves internal hosts while forwarding selected services. By the end you should be able to explain why a static route or a PBR rule was chosen, write the right nftables NAT rule, and verify packet flow. How would you choose between static routes, policy rules, or a routing daemon in your next design?

These objectives orient the practical skills you will practice. First, you will configure static routes and apply them where fixed, deterministic paths are safer and simpler than dynamic protocols. That matters when you need predictable paths to VPN peers, isolated subnets, or backup routers. Second, you will implement policy-based routing to steer traffic by source, interface, or user identity. PBR lets you keep multi‑homed servers predictable and isolate application traffic. Third, you will create advanced NAT configurations with nftables: SNAT and masquerade for outbound access and DNAT for port forwarding. You will learn when to use a specific public IP and when to rely on masquerading. Fourth, you will troubleshoot complex routing and NAT problems using the ip route, ip rule, and nftables inspection commands, plus packet capture to validate translations. Each objective includes why it matters and an example you can test in a lab so you leave with both understanding and repeatable commands.

This second objectives slide maps practice to verification. Learning begins with single-step static routes you add temporarily to see immediate path changes. Understanding comes next when you make routes persistent and reason about interface selection. Applying skills means creating PBR rules and custom routing tables so traffic from a specific host or process always takes a desired gateway. Finally, mastering the topic involves combining nftables NAT rules with PBR and verifying end-to-end flow with packet captures. For example, you will not only add a static route but also show how to persist it with a NetworkManager connection modification, and then confirm the kernel uses it with ip route get. A common misconception is that dynamic routing always replaces static routes; in practice architects choose static routes for predictable tunnels, and PBR when per-source behavior is required. Each objective card pairs a practical activity with a short mnemonic to help you recall the verification command for that skill.

Static routing is a manually configured instruction that tells the kernel to use a specific next hop for a destination. It is not learned from neighbors; it is authoritative and predictable. You use static routes for isolated subnets, tunnel endpoints, and simple failover where a deterministic path is required. For example, if a server must reach 10.0.0.0/24 through 192.168.1.254 on interface eth0, you add a static route that pins that traffic to that gateway. A frequent mistake is adding the route to the wrong interface or not persisting it, which causes problems after a reboot. Persisting a static route on RHEL often uses NetworkManager configuration so the route survives reconnects. Another misconception is that static routes are obsolete because dynamic routing exists; in practice, static routes are simpler and safer for single host policies and for ensuring control over particular flows. In this screen you'll see the command example and a persistence recipe; practice will help you move from adding transient routes to designing a stable routing table that supports VPNs and isolated services. Ask yourself: when would a static route be better than learning the path from a routing daemon?

Policy-based routing lets you make routing decisions using criteria other than the destination address. The two core components are ip rules and routing tables. An ip rule matches a condition — for example, a source address or a UID — and points to a named routing table. That table contains routes used only when the rule matches. A typical flow is: create a table entry in /etc/iproute2/rt_tables, add routes to that table, then create an ip rule to direct matching traffic to it. For example, traffic from 192.168.1.100 can be forced out a separate gateway, preserving the default route for other hosts. PBR is powerful for multi‑homed hosts, VPN exit selection, and isolating application traffic. A frequent pitfall is incorrect rule priority ordering or not verifying the rule with ip rule show; another is forgetting that policy rules are consulted before regular routing, so an overly broad rule can capture traffic unintentionally. Practice by adding a table, a route in that table, and an ip rule, then simulate a lookup with ip route get specifying the source to confirm behavior. Consider: which applications benefit most from PBR in your environment?

Source NAT changes the source address of outbound packets so replies return to the gateway and reach the original sender. In practice you either set a specific public address with SNAT or use masquerading when the outbound address is dynamic. Using nftables you place SNAT or masquerade rules in the postrouting chain of the nat table. For example, to translate 192.168.0.0/24 to a fixed public IP you write an snat rule; to automatically use whatever IP the interface holds you use masquerade. A common error is applying the rule to the wrong interface name or forgetting to enable IP forwarding in the kernel. For hands-on verification, load the ruleset and then use tcpdump on the external interface to confirm packets carry the translated source and check connection tracking entries. Below is the nftables rule example from the chapter for both specific SNAT and masquerade. Practice by toggling between a fixed snat address and masquerade to see how replies are handled when the external IP changes. nftables SNAT and Masquerade means snat sets a specific public ip; masquerade uses the interface ip dynamically. use masquerade for pppoe or dhcp-assigned public addresses.. In practical terms, configure source nat for outbound connectivity and understand masquerading. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Destination NAT changes the destination address of inbound packets so external clients can reach internal services. Use DNAT when you want to publish a web server behind a gateway. DNAT rules belong in the prerouting chain of the nat table because the destination must be rewritten before the kernel performs routing decisions. A correct DNAT includes matching the incoming interface, the gateway's public IP or any destination address, and the TCP port to forward. A typical error is forgetting to allow forwarded packets through the filter forward chain or neglecting to permit established and related states. After creating the rule, verify that the prerouting translation happens by listing the nftables ruleset and capturing packets on both external and internal interfaces to see original and translated destinations. The chapter includes a concrete example mapping external port 80 to an internal host on port 80; practice this with a non-production server and ensure firewall forward rules permit the flow. Think: what other services may require DNAT and what security controls should accompany them? DNAT and Port Forwarding with nftables means place dnat in prerouting, allow forwarding in filter chains, verify with nft list ruleset and tcpdump, and test service reachability from an external client.. In practical terms, expose internal services safely using prerouting dnat. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Network Prefix Translation for IPv6, known as NPTv6, maps one IPv6 prefix to another in a deterministic, reversible way. Unlike IPv4 NAT that rewrites host addresses arbitrarily, NPTv6 translates prefixes on a one-to-one basis, preserving the address scheme inside while allowing external renumbering or multi‑homing. This is useful when changing providers or when internal numbering must remain stable across provider changes. Because IPv6 has abundant addresses, NPTv6 is less common but still valuable in multi‑homed designs where you cannot use provider-independent addressing. nftables supports NPTv6 rules; implement them carefully since they affect routing and potential firewall policies. A misconception is expecting NPTv6 to behave like IPv4 NAT for port sharing — it is prefix based and intended for symmetry rather than hiding hosts. Test in a lab by translating an internal prefix to an external prefix, then validate with ping and tcpdump to confirm that address translations follow the expected mapping and that connection tracking reflects consistent state. NPTv6: IPv6 Prefix Translation means nptv6 maps one ipv6 prefix to another for renumbering or multi-homing; it is prefix-preserving and reversible, not a port-level nat.. In practical terms, when and how to translate ipv6 prefixes without traditional nat drawbacks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. As an RHCA you must know when to recommend dynamic routing daemons like OSPF or BGP versus host-level static or policy routing. OSPF is an interior gateway protocol used inside an autonomous system. It builds a link-state database so routers learn the network topology and compute shortest paths. BGP, in contrast, is an exterior gateway protocol used between autonomous systems; it shares path and policy information and selects routes based on path attributes and policy rather than shortest path metrics. A common design pattern is to let routers run OSPF inside a datacenter and use BGP between data centers or to the internet. However, for a single host or small gateway, running a routing daemon may add complexity; static routes or PBR are often simpler and more controllable. Misconception: BGP is not only for the internet; it is also used for large private networks requiring policy-based inter-domain routing. Think about scale, change rate, and policy needs when choosing between static, PBR, OSPF, or BGP. Troubleshooting advanced routing often requires stepping through the kernel's lookup process and verifying what actually hits the wire. Start with ip route get to ask the kernel which route it will use for a specific destination and source. This tells you the selected next hop and interface. Next, inspect ip rule show to see policy-based routing entries that might override the usual destination lookup. For NAT issues, run nft list ruleset to confirm your nat table has the expected prerouting and postrouting entries. Packet capture is the ultimate verification: run tcpdump on both internal and external interfaces to observe original and translated addresses. Watch connection tracking state as well; many NAT problems stem from ct state mismatches or stale entries. A common misconception is that the kernel will always pick the default route; in reality ip rules and table lookups can redirect traffic before the default is consulted. When a packet fails, simulate with ip route get from the source and run tcpdump to confirm whether the packet is leaving the expected interface. Keep a checklist: ip rule show, ip route show table, ip route get, nft list ruleset, tcpdump on both interfaces.

When you change routing or NAT on a production gateway, you must follow safe deployment patterns. First, always test in an isolated lab that mirrors interface names and gateway addresses. Use non-production IPs and verify rules with nft list ruleset and tcpdump. Second, persist configuration: ip route and ip rule changes are ephemeral, so write persistent entries via NetworkManager, system startup scripts, or the proper distro configuration so the system recovers after reboots or link flaps. Third, secure DNAT exposures: only forward needed ports and restrict source addresses where possible. Fourth, monitor connection tracking and stale states; NAT relies on a consistent connection tracking table and misconfigured firewall rules can cause half-open or broken connections. Common pitfalls include forgetting to enable ip forwarding, mis-typed interface names, and placing NAT rules in the wrong chain. Finally, include rollback steps and a maintenance window when you apply gateway changes. Let's review three essential concepts. First, a static route is a manually configured path that gives you deterministic routing to specific networks or hosts. Use it for tunnels and isolated subnets. Second, policy-based routing allows routing based on more than destination: source address, UID, or interface. PBR is indispensable for multi‑homed servers and segregating service traffic. Third, SNAT and masquerade change packet source addresses for outbound connections; masquerade is useful when the external IP is dynamic.
